items.question_text: A spring with a spring constant of \(100\,\text{N/m}\) is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality, to an extension of \(0.3\,\text{m}\). Calculate the energy stored in its elastic potential energy store. Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

wrong.misconception: This does not square the extension: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 0.3^{2} = 4.5\,\text{J}\).
This leaves out the half: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 0.3^{2} = 4.5\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: A spring has a natural length of \(12\,\text{cm}\). A mass hung from it stretches it to a length of \(20\,\text{cm}\). The spring constant is \(50\,\text{N/m}\). Calculate the energy stored in its elastic potential energy store. Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

wrong.misconception: This uses the stretched length, 20 cm. Use the extension: \(20 - 12 = 8\,\text{cm} = 0.08\,\text{m}\), so \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.08^{2} = 0.16\,\text{J}\).
This uses the extension in centimetres. Convert first: 8 cm = 0.08 m, so \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.08^{2} = 0.16\,\text{J}\).
This does not square the extension. \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.08^{2} = 0.16\,\text{J}\).
4 N is the force on the spring (\(F = ke = 50 \times 0.08\)), not the energy stored. \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2} = 0.16\,\text{J}\).

items.explanation: Extension = stretched length − natural length = 20 − 12 = 8 cm = 0.08 m. \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.08^{2} = 0.16\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: In which unit is the spring constant of a spring measured?

feedback.b: Joules measure energy, not the spring constant.
feedback.c: Newtons measure force; the spring constant is force per metre of extension.

misconception_map.c: slip: gave the unit of force
misconception_map.d: slip: gave the unit of mass

items.explanation: The spring constant is the force needed per metre of extension, so its unit is N/m.

items.question_text: When a spring is stretched by \(0.06\,\text{m}\), it stores \(0.9\,\text{J}\) in its elastic potential energy store. What is its spring constant? Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

feedback.a: This divides by the extension, not the extension squared. \(k = \dfrac{2E_e}{e^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.9}{0.06^{2}} = 500\,\text{N/m}\).
feedback.b: The half goes the other way when you rearrange: multiply the energy by 2. \(k = \dfrac{2E_e}{e^{2}} = 500\,\text{N/m}\).
feedback.c: This loses the 2 that comes from the half. \(k = \dfrac{2E_e}{e^{2}} = \dfrac{1.8}{0.0036} = 500\,\text{N/m}\).

items.question_text: The elastic band of a catapult has a spring constant of \(320\,\text{N/m}\). It is pulled back so that it stretches by \(0.25\,\text{m}\). How much energy is stored in its elastic potential energy store? Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

feedback.c: This does not square the extension. \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 320 \times 0.25^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 320 \times 0.0625 = 10\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: 80 is the force on the band in newtons (\(F = ke = 320 \times 0.25\)), not the energy stored. \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2} = 10\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: Springs X and Y are stretched by the same extension. Spring X has twice the spring constant of spring Y. How does the energy stored in X compare with Y? Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

options.c: X stores four times as much

feedback.a: The extension is the same, so the energy stored is the same.
feedback.c: Only the extension is squared, and it is the same for both.
feedback.d: A spring with a smaller spring constant does not store more energy for the same extension.

misconception_map.a: slip: thinks the spring constant changes the energy
misconception_map.d: slip: inverted the relationship with k

items.explanation: With the same extension, both springs store the same energy.

items.question_text: A spring is stretched, and then stretched again to twice the extension. It stays within its limit of proportionality. How does the energy in its elastic potential energy store change? Use \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}\).

options.a: It doubles, because the extension doubles
options.b: It becomes four times as large
options.c: It stays the same, because the spring constant does not change
options.d: It becomes twice as large, because ½ × 2² = 2

feedback.a: The energy depends on the extension squared, not the extension. Doubling e multiplies e² by 4, so the energy is four times as large.
feedback.c: The spring constant stays the same, but the extension has changed. The energy depends on e², so it becomes four times as large.
feedback.d: The ½ is in both the old and the new energy, so it cancels in the comparison. Only the 2² remains: the energy becomes four times as large.

misconception_map.c: slip: thinks the energy stored depends only on the spring constant
misconception_map.d: slip: applied the ½ to the ratio instead of to each energy

items.explanation: The energy stored is proportional to the extension squared (Ee = ½ke², with k fixed). Doubling the extension multiplies it by 2² = 4.
